accordion.use: The accordion component is used to organise and display content in collapsible sections. It allows users to toggle the visibility of content areas, helping manage dense information and reduce cognitive load.
variants: Basic — for simple sections and grouped content, e.g. driver details or FAQ
Detailed — for complex content or multiple levels of information, e.g. policy details
anatomy: Basic — Border, Background surface, Label, Icon (closed); when open: Content zone, Divider, Icon (open)
Detailed — Border, Lozenge component, Icon (closed), Large vector icon, Label, Heading; when open: Content zone, Icon (open)
size: Basic — padding top/bottom spacing-md, padding left/right spacing-md, gap spacing-md (open: content padding top/bottom spacing-md, left/right spacing-md)

Detailed — padding top/bottom spacing-md, left/right spacing-md, image-to-content gap spacing-md, icon gap spacing-md, lozenge-to-content gap spacing-xs (open: content padding top/bottom spacing-md, left/right spacing-md)
Touch target at least 44×44px on mobile
characterLimit: Titles — maximum 60 characters (avoid truncation on small screens)
Content — should fit within 3–5 paragraphs; break large blocks into multiple accordion items
states: Hover — container highlights to indicate interactivity
Focus — visible focus ring for keyboard navigation
Active (table) — content fully revealed, table format
transitions: Ease-out for expansion, ease-in for collapse [TBC]
More than one accordion may be expanded at a time [TBC]
accessibility: Use a semantic <button> for triggers
Apply aria-expanded="true/false" to indicate state
Group accordion content with aria-controls and id
Ensure content is focusable and screen-reader friendly
Keyboard: Tab between headers, Enter/Space to toggle
doList: Present large amounts of related information in a compact space
Use meaningful, concise titles
Group related content logically
Ensure visual indicators match the state
dontList: Use when all information must be visible at once
Use when the content is critical for completing a task
Use when the expanded content is very short
Nest accordions within accordions
Use as a substitute for page navigation
Hide essential information users must always see
accordion.sourceIssue: The live site's Do list includes "Use accordions when all the information must be visible at once" — the same line also appears in the Don't list, which is clearly the intended rule. Read as a copy-paste duplication in the source and removed from Do here rather than silently kept.

alert.use: To attract a user's attention with important messages or required actions.
variants: Size: Standard, Mini, Mobile, Mini mobile
Information — general information
Confirmation — confirms an action or success
Warning — a minor warning
Error — a critical error has occurred
Change — a tip or non-critical change
anatomy: Container — wraps the content
Icon — supports the variant meaning (circle-info / circle-check / triangle-exclamation / circle-exclamation / lightbulb)
Title — conveys what triggered the alert
Description (optional) — purpose and next steps, can include in-text links
Dismissal (optional) — permanently removes the alert
Actions (optional) — links to remedy the alert or continue a task
size: Standard: 24px padding, 24px between things, 6px between text
Mini: 12–18px padding, 12px between things, 6px between text
Mobile: 24px padding, 12px between things, 6px between text
Mini mobile: 12–18px padding, 12px between things, 6px between text
All fill container width, hug content height
typography: Standard & mobile — Title Bold/16px|22px P2/100; Description Regular/14px|20px P2/100; Actions Underline/14px|20px Interaction/Link; Icon FA6 Pro Regular 24px P2/100; Dismiss FA6 Pro Solid 14px P2/60.
Mini & mini mobile — Title Medium/14px|20px P2/100; Actions Underline/14px|20px Interaction/Link; Icon FA6 Pro Regular 18px P2/100; Dismiss FA6 Pro Solid 14px P2/60.
characterLimit: Standard & mobile: under 60 characters should use the mini variant instead
states: Skeleton — shown while the component is loading
transitions: Animation on skeleton load, then transitions into the real alert type
priority: Alerts appear in priority order: 1. Error, 2. Warning, 3. Information, 4. Change
accessibility: Actions and dismiss button must be focusable
Don't rely on colour alone — provide an accessible label for the type/icon
Dynamic alerts should use the alert role (a live region that doesn't take focus)
Minimum touch target 48×48px for actions and dismiss
No fixed height — text must be able to zoom/resize
doList: Make error messages clear and concise
Use the correct variant for the content length and device
dontList: Restyle with other colours or icons
Use multiple icons
Use buttons instead of links for actions
Write too much
Change the icon
Use a basic alert without a description
Use a mini alert without a description

Alert's real description above is the one we confirmed earlier and kept.

button.use: Buttons on a website serve as interactive elements that enable users to perform actions or navigate through the site. They are a crucial component of a website's user interface and user experience, providing clear and intuitive means for interaction.
variants: Primary, secondary, icon left/right, icon only, text, selected, error, details, back-to-top, loading
anatomy: The anatomy of a button contains a background colour, border, label, and optional icon. The icon may be on the left or right of the label, or it may be an icon-only button depending on context. The border, label, icon, and background surface depend on the button type and interaction state.
1. Border, 2. Background surface, 3. Label, 4. Icon
button.tokenCrossCheck: spacing/sm and spacing/md match the real Spacing foundation scale exactly (spacing-sm = 12px, spacing-md = 24px) — a genuine cross-confirmation between two independent sources. But the real captured code still shows these as raw pixel values with NO TOKEN BOUND — meaning the documentation names the intended token, while the actual implementation hasn't wired it up yet. That's a real implementation gap, not a correction to the earlier finding.

types.title: Primary
types.body: Used for the most important call to action. States: Default, Hover, Focus, Active.

types.title: Secondary
types.body: Used for secondary actions.

types.title: Icon buttons
types.body: Icons are used to inform the functionality of the button, not for decoration.

states: Feedback states: loading, error, or selected/success — used to reflect the interface's status after a click
transitions: Loading transition hides the label during the loading animation
arrangement: Align buttons right/left in modals and drawers
Align to the left in page navigation
accessibility: Using two primary buttons together can cause confusion and dilute the call to action — use one primary button for the most critical action, and a secondary or link style for less critical ones, to maintain clear visual hierarchy
Ensure buttons are accessible to screen reader users — use aria-labels if the button text alone doesn't provide enough context

Avoid disabling buttons — instead allow the interaction and show an error message with instructions on how to proceed. (Source notes disabled buttons may still be appropriate during an active loading animation — open question.)
doList: Use primary and secondary/text together
Use an icon left/right or icon only
Use one icon per button
dontList: Use multiple primary buttons together
Place an icon both left and right
Allow the label to wrap to multiple lines
Use multiple icons in a single button

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear, actionable, and concise language
contentGuidelines.body: Precisely convey the action taken on click; keep text to roughly one to three words so it fits and stays readable. Start with a verb ("Submit", "Download", "Buy Now", "Learn More"). Avoid technical jargon.

contentGuidelines.title: Be consistent
contentGuidelines.body: Maintain consistent terminology, capitalisation, and verb forms across buttons, plus consistent colour and shape, so users recognise buttons easily.

contentGuidelines.title: Consider hierarchy
contentGuidelines.body: Use size, colour, or placement to prioritise buttons when there are several on a page — a primary and secondary pairing establishes clear hierarchy.

contentGuidelines.title: Provide feedback
contentGuidelines.body: Give immediate feedback on click — colour/shape change or a loading animation — to confirm the action is processing. Use hover effects to signal clickability.

behaviour: Loading transition hides the label during the loading animation
button.usedInPattern: Common Actions (referenced in the source as a real Pattern this component belongs to — Patterns haven't been captured in this system yet, so this is a forward reference, not a broken link)

breadcrumb.use: The Breadcrumbs component provides users with contextual information about their location within a product's hierarchy. It improves navigation, particularly on deep pages, and reduces the need for backtracking by offering quick access to previous levels.
variants: Primary — plain text with separators (e.g. "My Account home / My Road Service / Road Service details")
With icons — leading icons to improve scannability
Overflow — collapses intermediate items into a dropdown when space is limited
Current page is non-clickable by default
anatomy: Container — horizontal flex container
Items — each breadcrumb item, typically a text link
Separator — plain text with /
Current item — last item on the right, styled distinctly and not clickable
size: Width — responsive, fits container or truncates with overflow logic
Collapses on mobile to save space
typography: Primary and sub item — Underline/14px | 20px, P2/100
Should scale dynamically with accessibility settings or screen size
characterLimit: If exceeded, truncate with an ellipsis, with full text accessible via tooltip or an alternative method
states: Default, hover, focus, active/pressed, disabled, selected
transitions: Fade or slide animations between states
arrangement: On small screens, prioritise essential content and reduce horizontal padding
accessibility: Keyboard navigable — reachable via Tab
Use aria-current, aria-disabled, aria-label appropriately
Meets WCAG AA colour contrast (4.5:1 minimum)
Visible focus indicators
Layout must not break at up to 200% zoom
doList: Use consistent spacing and clear labels
Provide accessible labels for screen readers
Indicate the current item with aria-current="page"
Use clear, plain language reflecting the real hierarchy
Be consistent in naming, capitalisation, and punctuation
Truncate thoughtfully, with full text available via tooltip
dontList: Make all breadcrumb items look the same
Truncate without a tooltip or way to access the full text
Rely on colour alone to indicate state
tokens: Gaps left and right between items — spacing/xs

date.use: The date component enables people to select a date, or a range of dates. See the date validation pattern definition for validation rules.
principles: The user must always have ultimate control
The user must be able to edit with ease
The cursor must not be hijacked — e.g. jumped to the end of a field or to another field
The user must not be forced to enter preceding '0's (e.g. 01) to make a form valid — zero-padding should only happen behind the scenes after submission, never somewhere the user can see it
The solution must support autocomplete where possible
The user must not be forced to use a date picker/calendar
variants: Significant date (no picker) — for a date that's easily recalled or referenced, e.g. birth date. Max width 282px.
Choose date (picker available) — for a date within ~6 months, where the day of week may matter. Max width 282px.
Date range (range picker available) — for a start and end date.
anatomy: Day, Month, Year fields
Picker button (icon)
Calendar picker — single month view (Choose date) or two month view (Date range)
Select Year, month navigation arrows, month & year label, weekday labels, days
size: The component should not be stretched to fit a container
Field sizes are fixed based on the input required, to indicate character limits to the user
On very narrow screens, fields stack vertically with left alignment
typography: Calendar — month/year label Semibold/14px|20px P2/100; days & years Regular/14px|20px P2/100; weekday labels Regular/12px|18px P2/50
characterLimit: Single-character day/month input should be translated to 01-style format before submission
states: Fields: default, hover, active, focus, disabled, value (filled), invalid
accessibility: The Date label should be the legend of the field set, with day/month/year as form elements
Validation errors must be associated with the correct field(s), including via aria-describedby
doList: Enable single-digit entry for day or month
Apply a max width of 282px for Significant date and Choose date
Fill in both dates from the picker when a range is selected
Pre-fill information if known
dontList: Stretch the component to fit a container
resources: GOV.UK date input pattern (accessibility, field set, code examples)
Adam Silver — multiple inputs vs one input

checkbox-basic.use: Checkboxes allow users to select one or multiple options from a list. They are ideal for toggling individual features on or off, or for selecting multiple items for bulk actions.
variants: Basic — simple forms or single-item selections
Checkbox List (Vertical) — filtering lists, multi-select menus
Checkbox (Horizontal) — grouping options, e.g. inside cards or tiles
Checkbox Horizontal (Mobile) — mobile-friendly selection
anatomy: Checkbox input — clickable control showing checked/unchecked state
Label — beside the checkbox
Count (optional) — indicates quantities of list items
Container (optional) — visual boundary
size: Touch target at least 44×44px on mobile
accessibility: The clickable area must include both the checkbox and its label
Use native <input type="checkbox"> where possible
aria-checked="true/false" on custom checkboxes
aria-invalid="true" for error states
Proper label association via <label for="id">
Minimum touch target 44×44px including padding
doList: Pair checkboxes with clear, descriptive labels
Keep labels short — use an info link or help text for more detail
Group related checkboxes logically
Use validation states to give feedback
dontList: Nest checkboxes in interactive elements like buttons or links
Hide important validation feedback
Place checkboxes too close together

journey-footer.use: RAA's design system includes three footer types, each optimised for a specific use case: the Journey footer, the Sticky footer, and the Site footer.
variants: Journey footer — contextual footer used in insurance quote journeys to guide users through steps
Sticky footer — persistent floating footer for continuity when scrolling (not yet captured as its own component in this session)
Site footer — informational footer used across all pages
anatomy: Journey footer — hairline top divider (1px, P2/100), left-aligned primary button, optional right-aligned "Next step" text, optional right-aligned "Skip for now" text button. Desktop horizontal, pinned; mobile vertical stack, full-width button.

Sticky footer — floating container, 1px P2/100 border, 4px radius, left-aligned primary button, right-aligned "Next step", background P3/100 at 92% opacity with 4px blur, drop shadow (0/12/48/0, P2/100 10%).
accessibility: All footer content keyboard accessible in a logical flow
Text links meet WCAG 2.1 AA contrast (4.5:1)
Semantic HTML — <footer> site-wide, <nav>/<div> for sticky/journey containers
Buttons need descriptive aria-label if text is ambiguous
Sticky elements must not obscure key content on small screens
Minimum touch target 44×44px
doList: Use the Journey footer to clearly guide users to the next step
Use consistent spacing and divider rules across footer types
Adapt layout for smaller screens
dontList: Overload the footer with too much content
Let sticky footers block fixed-position elements (e.g. the chat widget)
tokens: Journey footer — spacing/md padding top, spacing/md button padding L/R, spacing/sm button padding T/B, spacing/2xl+ gap to "Next: Step" text
Site footer — spacing/md top/bottom padding, spacing/lg left/right padding, spacing/xs link-to-icon gap, spacing/md link-to-footer-text gap
QTB footer — spacing/md throughout, spacing/2xl+ gap between button and footer text

site-footer.use: The informational footer used across all web pages — one of RAA's three footer types.
anatomy: Link group (Privacy Policy, Cookies Policy, Terms & Conditions) with dot dividers (6px horizontal padding)
Copyright text
Background matches the section above: P1/100, P3/100, or S2/30
Desktop horizontal centred; Tablet vertical stack centred; Mobile vertical stack left-aligned with a 0.8px P2/30 divider

header-desktop.use: The header sits at the top of the page and provides quick access to navigation, branding, and key actions like search or user profile. It should be consistent, responsive, and accessible across all devices.
anatomy: Header — logo, section title, flexible space, "Need help" label, help icon
QTB Header — price, billing info, spacer/alignment zone, call-to-action button
size: Help icon to Log out button gap — spacing-md
Log out button padding — 12px vertical, 24px horizontal
QTB header — spacing-md left/right, spacing-sm price-to-description, spacing-md top/bottom
typography: QTB price — Bold/36px | 40px; "per month" Bold/14px|20px; "or $X per year" Regular/14px|20px
behaviour: "Saving..." / "Saved just now" give real-time autosave feedback, removing the need for a manual Save button — may fade after a few seconds or stay subtly visible
tokens: Gap help icon to Log out button — spacing/md
QTB header — spacing/md left/right/top/bottom, spacing/xs price-to-description gap
accessibility: Fully keyboard navigable with screen reader support and sufficient colour contrast
Clear focus states and descriptive aria-labels on interactive elements
Logo links to the homepage with alt text
Use navigation landmarks (<header>, role="banner")
doList: Keep the header responsive across screen sizes
Use semantic HTML/ARIA roles
Provide meaningful alt text for the logo
Maintain consistent layout and hierarchy across pages
dontList: Overload the header with too many actions or links
Use non-descriptive labels/icons without alternatives
Rely solely on colour to convey information
Hide critical navigation on small screens without an accessible alternative

text-field-regular.use: Users can enter text shorter than a single line. Input fields can have multiple input types depending on the use case: text, tel (phone number), email, number (postcode, bank details), or password (input obscured as the user types).
variants: Default, value, invalid, valid, icon left, icon right
anatomy: Label
Container
Text (optional)
Prefix icon (optional)
Suffix icon (optional)
Description (optional)
size: 6px spacing between label, container and description
typography: Icon — Font Awesome 6 Pro Regular 24px, P2/100
Invalid: Invalid/100. Valid: Valid/100. Disabled: P2/40.
characterLimit: Single line, no truncation — make it scrollable or use a text area for long input
transitions: Animation on active and focus states
arrangement: 24px margin between input fields and nearby components
Field width should match how much information is needed
Inline layout for side-by-side fields on larger screens; full width on mobile
accessibility: Avoid placeholder text where possible — it disappears once typing starts, isn't always read by screen readers, and often lacks contrast
Use prefixes/suffixes for things like currency, but don't rely on them alone — say the format in the label/hint text too

Match the input type to the data (e.g. type="tel")
Announce inline validation errors and focus the field in error
Give specific error messages that explain the fix
Communicate expected format and validate it
Keep tab order logical

Use an asterisk for mandatory/optional — write '(optional)' instead
Use placeholder text
Truncate text
Disable copy and paste
Hijack the cursor during input
Use placeholder text for instructions
Write error messages that don't explain the fix

input-counter.use: An input counter shows the number of characters entered, or lets a user increment/decrement a numeric value, helping them stay within a set limit (e.g. "16 / 99"). It updates in real time and may show a warning when a limit is exceeded.
anatomy: Decrement button (−)
Value display (current number)
Increment button (+)
accessibility: Operable by keyboard and screen readers
Each button needs a clear aria-label ('Increase value' / 'Decrease value')
Current value exposed via an aria-live region or a labelled editable input
Visible focus indicators, minimum touch target 44×44px
Use role="spinbutton" with aria-valuenow/aria-valuemin/aria-valuemax
doList: Label buttons and fields clearly — not vague terms like 'More'/'Less'
Pair the counter with a visible label explaining what's being counted
Keep the value format consistent
Communicate min/max limits clearly
Support manual entry where flexibility is needed
Use plain, action-oriented language
Reflect state changes immediately
dontList: Use icons without accessible labels
Rely solely on colour for feedback
Hide value changes from screen readers
Allow the counter to exceed its limits

information-drawer.use: The information drawer is a flyout panel that opens when a user clicks a link, providing additional contextual information to assist with completing a task.
anatomy: A background container with a drop shadow
A close button
A title/heading(s)
Body copy — can contain lists, links & subheadings
behaviour: Animates in and out from the right side of the page
Enables scroll within the panel
Users can click the page background or close icon to dismiss (desktop)
Users can swipe to close (mobile)
A blanket overlays the main site in the background while open
accessibility: Minimum size for the close icon — 44×44px
Treat as a flyout — keyboard tabbing should stay within the flyout, not the background page; avoid a keyboard trap
Announce the open action to screen reader users
If chat is available, ensure the drawer doesn't hide the chat button when open
doList: Support keyboard navigation and screen reader announcements
Always open on the right side on desktop; animate in from the right to fill the screen on mobile
Let users close via the close icon, Esc, clicking the background (desktop), or swipe (mobile)
Fit the drawer height to the viewport and allow scroll for longer content
dontList: Use the drawer for mandatory instructions — if users must read it to proceed, put it on the main page
Open multiple drawers at once — only one should be active at a time

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear, action-driven link text
contentGuidelines.body: The text that opens the drawer should say plainly what it does.

contentGuidelines.title: Keep content concise and relevant
contentGuidelines.body: Only what supports the field or section it's attached to.

contentGuidelines.title: Use plain language
contentGuidelines.body: Easy for users of all levels to understand.

contentGuidelines.title: Don't overload the drawer
contentGuidelines.body: It's for supplemental info, not full documentation.

banner.use: Banners highlight important messages at the top of a page. They use clear icons, colours, and concise text to communicate status or actions, such as information, warnings, or success. Banners can include links or buttons and may be dismissible.
anatomy: A container holding an icon, a concise message, and optional actions (buttons or links). Distinct colours indicate the message type — informational, warning, success, or error. Some banners include a close/dismiss button.
1. Background, 2. Step text, 3. Title
accessibility: Clear, concise language and sufficient colour contrast (WCAG AA)
Icons must not rely on colour alone — pair with descriptive text/labels
Screen reader announcement via role="alert" (critical) or role="status" (less urgent)
Dismiss buttons keyboard accessible and clearly labelled
doList: Keep the message brief, clear, and actionable
Use the correct banner type with matching colours and icons
Meet accessibility requirements — contrast, screen reader announcement, keyboard-accessible actions
Provide a dismiss option for non-critical banners
dontList: Overuse banners or place multiple on the same page
Rely on colour alone to communicate meaning
Include detailed or lengthy content inside a banner
Use banners for low-priority or permanent information

contentGuidelines.title: Be clear and concise
contentGuidelines.body: Focus on the essential information users need to know or act on immediately.

contentGuidelines.title: Use an appropriate tone
contentGuidelines.body: Helpful and positive for informational/success; clear but calm for warnings/errors — never alarming.

contentGuidelines.title: Prioritise key information first
contentGuidelines.body: Users should understand the purpose at a glance.

contentGuidelines.title: Guide users toward action when needed
contentGuidelines.body: Use specific, action-oriented language ("Update Now") not vague terms ("Click Here").

contentGuidelines.title: Keep messages relevant and timely
contentGuidelines.body: Remove or update banners as soon as the information changes.

contentGuidelines.title: Support accessibility
contentGuidelines.body: Icons and text labels must always work together to communicate the message.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid overuse
contentGuidelines.body: Too many banners cause users to start ignoring them.

types.title: Banner
types.body: A prominent text area — step indicator plus a bold title — over a strong, bright gradient background, used to grab attention and convey progress or headings.

types.title: Banner Base
types.body: A background-only visual element — a curved gradient with no text, acting as a decorative foundation behind content or sections.

filters.use: Filters help users narrow down content by selecting specific criteria. They appear as dropdowns, checkboxes, or toggles, depending on context. Filters should be clear, easy to adjust, and consistently placed for quick access across devices.
anatomy: A label describing the filter category, filter controls (checkboxes, toggles, dropdowns), and a clear/reset button. Active filters show as tags or chips for easy review and removal. Layout may adjust to a panel, drawer, or dropdown on smaller devices.
1. Filter name, 2. Clear all filters, 3. Pull-down menu
Price range filter — 1. Slider selector, 2. Price parameter
Checkbox filter — 1. Filter label, 2. Ticked/unticked label, 3. Show all
accessibility: Range filter: keyboard-accessible slider (arrow keys, tab), visible focus indicators, clear "Minimum"/"Maximum" labels programmatically linked for screen readers
ARIA attributes on the slider — aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, aria-valuenow, aria-label
Sufficient colour contrast; error messaging announced via aria-live where needed
Touch targets meet the minimum recommended size for mobile
doList: Use clear and descriptive labels
Make filters accessible via keyboard and screen reader with ARIA attributes and visible focus indicators
Keep filters responsive with touch-friendly controls
Display active filters clearly and allow easy removal
Group related filters logically; validate input with accessible error messages
dontList: Rely on colour alone to communicate filter states
Hide filter labels or make users guess their purpose
Overwhelm users with too many unorganised filter options
Force a strict filtering order
Design filters that are difficult to use on smaller screens

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear labels
contentGuidelines.body: Filter names must be simple, direct, and clearly describe what they do.

contentGuidelines.title: Be specific
contentGuidelines.body: "Price Range" or "Kilometres", not vague terms like "Amount".

contentGuidelines.title: Keep it concise
contentGuidelines.body: Short labels and options; extra detail goes in tooltips or help text.

contentGuidelines.title: Match user language
contentGuidelines.body: Avoid internal terminology users won't recognise.

contentGuidelines.title: Use consistent capitalisation
contentGuidelines.body: Sentence case across all filter labels and options.

contentGuidelines.title: Group related options
contentGuidelines.body: e.g. "Vehicle Type" or "Coverage Level" categories.

contentGuidelines.title: Provide default values carefully
contentGuidelines.body: Only pre-select if it improves the experience — never force confusing defaults.

contentGuidelines.title: Show active filters clearly
contentGuidelines.body: Displayed with an easy way to remove or adjust them.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid jargon
contentGuidelines.body: Filters should feel accessible regardless of technical knowledge.

contentGuidelines.title: Support error prevention
contentGuidelines.body: Hint text, examples, or tooltips for filters needing user input (sliders, numeric fields).

progress-linear.use: Progress indicators let people know that your screen isn't stalled while it loads content or performs lengthy operations. A progress tracker visually guides users through a series of steps required to complete a multi-step task, typically across multiple screens — it helps set expectations, reduce cognitive load, and improve task completion.
anatomy: Linear — 1. Active indicator, 2. Track, 3. Stop indicator, 4. Tooltip (on hover), 5. Step
Radial — determinate (well-defined duration, e.g. a file conversion) or indeterminate (unquantifiable, e.g. loading/syncing)
size: Radial sizes — Small 24×24px (compact elements, buttons, form fields), Medium 48×48px (default, most use cases), Large 96×96px (prominent loading states, full-screen views)
doList: Use a progress tracker when there are three or more steps
Let people navigate by selecting a step in the sequence
Use circular indicators for short, indeterminate activities under 5 seconds
Simplify or split a process that needs more than six steps
Use a "Next" button instead of a tracker if there are fewer than three steps
dontList: Use a linear bar loading indicator inside a button
Switch from the circular style to the bar style mid-flow — they're different shapes and switching disrupts the interface
Freeze a circular indicator — it can make the process look stalled
accessibility: Use a label describing the process occurring (e.g. "loading", "submitting", "processing")
Circular indicators don't reduce motion — a frozen spinner reads as a stopped process
behaviour: Determinate indicators should show a consistent pace — jumping to 90% quickly then stalling on the last 10% erodes trust
Keep progress indicators moving so people know something is still happening; if paused, give feedback explaining why
Add a short, specific description where possible — avoid vague terms like "loading" or "authenticating" with no context
Spinners animate in by default; use a fade-in for a smoother exit rather than a sudden snap
progress-linear.tokenCrossCheck: The documented radial sizes (24px/48px/96px for Small/Medium/Large) match Spinner's real captured code exactly — a genuine cross-confirmation between documentation and shipped implementation.

lozenge.use: A lozenge is a visual indicator used to highlight an item's status for quick recognition.
accessibility: Don't use colour alone to signify an important state — use an accurate label too (e.g. "Error" or "Warning" for a critical status)
Don't use lozenges for long text — they aren't focusable, so any text truncated past 200px (or a custom maxWidth) won't be accessible
doList: Use a single, purposeful icon when it enhances meaning or scan-ability, with a clear semantic relationship to the text
Include a text label always, unless the icon is universally recognised and accessible on its own
Use concise text so the lozenge stays readable and accessible
dontList: Use multiple icons — this confuses users about the lozenge's function
Use an icon purely for decoration
Let text truncate — truncated text can't be focused or read by assistive technology
size: Default max width — 200px, truncates with an ellipsis past that; customisable via a maxWidth property

types.title: Primary
types.body: Used for the most important call to action.

types.title: Secondary
types.body: Used for secondary actions.

types.title: Tertiary
types.body: Used for passive actions.

step-item-horizontal.use: A stepper guides users through a multi-step process in an organised and intuitive manner, providing clarity and reducing cognitive load, letting them focus on one task at a time. It offers visual feedback on progress and lets users revisit prior steps if adjustments are needed.
anatomy: A step number and title, plus a progress track. The track's state aligns to the step number/title's state below it. The step number changes to a check icon once complete.
1. Step number, 2. Step title, 3. Progress Track
size: Space between step number and title — 6px
typography: Complete step number — Font Awesome 6 Pro/14px | 20px
accessibility: Use <nav> or <ol> to group the stepper, <li> for individual steps
Each step needs a clear, descriptive label conveying its purpose
Use aria-current="step" for the current step
Use aria-labelledby/aria-label to associate each step with its description
Consider role="progressbar" if the stepper reflects progress quantitatively
Keyboard-navigable (Tab, Shift+Tab)
Announce status updates (e.g. "Step 2 of 5 completed") via aria-live
doList: Ensure the step corresponds to the page title/step subtitle
Visually highlight the current step
Implement ARIA attributes and full keyboard/screen reader navigation
Permit navigating back to previous steps unless there's a specific reason not to
Limit the number of steps to what's necessary
dontList: Add unnecessary steps or overly complex instructions
Ignore loading states — show a visual indicator if a step involves loading time
Block progress without feedback on what needs correcting
Assume users will remember details from previous steps without a summary or review option
behaviour: The active state's step number has a slight animated outer glow
step-item-horizontal.tokenCrossCheck: The documented "active state glow" matches StepItemHorizontal's real captured code exactly — its Active state uses a feMorphology dilate filter for a soft yellow glow. Confirmed, not just documented.

skeleton.use: A skeleton acts as a placeholder for content, usually while it loads, to improve the perceived loading experience. Instead of a blank screen or a traditional spinner, it shows a placeholder layout that mimics the structure of the content that will eventually load.
anatomy: Darker grey bars indicate where content will load, regardless of background. A blank skeleton matches the dimensions of the component it represents; a text skeleton suits text with no background; a text-on-background skeleton suits larger text-in-container components; a skeleton with an image suits card/tile components.
Blank — 1. Grey skeleton box
Text — 1. Title and content skeleton
Text on background — 1. Background, 2. Skeleton text
With image — 1. Skeleton card image, 2. Skeleton text on background
accessibility: Use semantic HTML that gives context to assistive technologies
Use aria-busy="true" to signal loading
Provide meaningful text alternatives/descriptions indicating content is loading
Manage keyboard focus correctly — never trap or lose it within a skeleton
Inform users if loading will take a long time, with a progress indicator if feasible
Respect reduced-motion preferences
doList: Use skeletons to indicate where and what type of content will appear
Match the skeleton's layout to the actual content to avoid confusing users when it loads
Display skeletons immediately to reassure users the page is loading
Keep skeletons lightweight so they don't hinder load performance
Use them only where they genuinely enhance the experience
dontList: Use skeletons on every single element
Leave users staring at a skeleton indefinitely if content fails to load — provide a fallback
Use a static skeleton with no animation — it can read as frozen content
Use a skeleton when content loads almost instantly — it can slow the perception of speed
behaviour: A "shimmer effect" — a subtle gradient overlay moving left to right — animates during loading

types.title: Sizing rule
types.body: The skeleton's width and height should precisely match the content, component, or image it represents, for a seamless transition once loading completes.

skeleton.tokenCrossCheck: The documented spacing (24px padding, 6px gap) matches Skeleton's real captured code exactly ("Text on bg: p-[24px] gap-[6px]") — a genuine cross-confirmation, not just a coincidence.

link-back.use: Links are used as navigational elements. They navigate users to another location, such as a different site, resource, or section within the same page.
whenToUse: Open related material (like information drawers or documents)
Navigate to an entirely different site
Jump to an element on the same page
Link to emails or phone numbers
variants: Confirmed on a second real pass as four types: Internal link, External link, Back link, Information link — the first pass's longer list (download link, comparison table link, etc.) may be older/broader; treating this shorter list as the current canonical set.
anatomy: A link always includes link text and can have an icon.
1. Link text, 2. Icon (optional)
size: Keep links large enough to interact with — link targets should be at least 24×24px
typography: Icon — Font Awesome 6 Pro Regular/14px | 20px, Interaction/Link
characterLimit: See Do/Don't for guidance on link length
arrangement: Links with an icon: used on their own or directly following content. Align the icon to the text baseline when it spans more than one line. 6px spacing between text and icon.
In-text link: used within a sentence or paragraph — should not be paired with an icon.
accessibility: Open links in a new tab when there's a risk of someone losing their current place or task (e.g. insurance QTB journeys), or when the link takes them out of the current product / to an external site
Include an external link icon for standalone links for sighted users, and provide a visually hidden warning for screen readers
Links must be keyboard-navigable, receive focus when tabbed to, and have a clear focus state
doList: Ensure link text is descriptive and meaningful, understandable even out of context
Specify if a link triggers a download, including file type and size
Only include a verb in the linked text if it better describes the purpose or differentiates it from other links/actions
Maintain consistent styling (underlines, colour changes) so links are easily distinguishable
dontList: Confuse links and buttons
Use vague phrases like "Click here" or the URL as link text
Repeat the same link text over and over on a page
Include unnecessary links — too many can overwhelm a page, particularly for screen reader users
Create circular links that may frustrate or disorient the user
link-back.usedInPattern: Common Actions (same real Pattern Button belongs to — Patterns haven't been captured in this system yet)

helper.use: Helper is a friendly illustration of a female with a headset with microphone, symbolising support and communication. Often used as a chatbot or web avatar, she adds a warm, human touch to digital help.
anatomy: The anatomy of Helper includes a female icon with a purple circle background and a defined border. The icon may appear to the right of the page, as an avatar in a chatbot, and/or as a standalone avatar at the top of a header. Its size and background surface are flexible, adapting based on where and how it's used.
1. Helper Icon (Avatar)
2. Chat Bubble

Character detail — Headset: yellow with mic and earpiece. Hair: black, curly. Face: white skin, dot eyes, smiling mouth. Shirt: yellow with white collar. Background: purple circle with black border. Style: flat, simple, cartoon-like.
size: 32px for tooltips or tight spaces, 48px for standard UI help, 64px for onboarding or key help areas, 80px for prominent cards, 96px for hero sections or tutorials — choose based on visibility needs and layout space
Maintain 12px spacing between the helper icon and the chat box for clear separation and visual balance

types.title: Helper icon
types.body: A generic symbol (such as a question mark or info icon) used to represent quick tips or additional guidance inline within the interface.

types.title: Chatbot face
types.body: A character-style avatar that adds a human-like presence to messages, often used in conversational UI. Use the Helper Icon for subtle, non-conversational cues, and the Chatbot Face when the tone is more interactive or story-driven.

behaviour: The optimal transition duration to display a helper is around 200–300ms — quick enough to feel responsive, slow enough not to feel abrupt. A fade-in or slide-in transition works best, using easing like ease-out or ease-in-out.
accessibility: To meet WCAG 2.2, the helper icon should include descriptive alt text (e.g. "Support icon with smiling face and headset"), have sufficient contrast, and not rely on visuals alone to convey meaning
Use semantic elements (e.g. <div role="button"> or <a>) with proper ARIA labels
Fully keyboard navigable — Tab to focus, Enter/Space to activate, Esc to close
Use aria-live for updates and aria-current="page" for active help topics
Don't rely on colour alone — add icons or text
doList: Use the helper icon to visually reinforce support-related content, but never rely on it alone to convey meaning
Always provide descriptive alt text or pair the icon with a visible label
Ensure sufficient colour contrast and consistent sizing across devices
dontList: Use the icon as a button unless it has defined functionality and meets accessibility requirements
Change its meaning in different contexts without clear explanation

contentGuidelines.title: Be Friendly and Approachable
contentGuidelines.body: Use a warm, conversational tone. Avoid overly formal or robotic language. e.g. "Hi! How can I help you today?" not "Please state your inquiry."

contentGuidelines.title: Be Context-Aware
contentGuidelines.body: Tailor responses to the page or task the user is currently working on.

contentGuidelines.title: Guide, Don't Overwhelm
contentGuidelines.body: Break complex processes into small steps. Offer next-step suggestions and links to related help articles.

contentGuidelines.title: Respect User Attention
contentGuidelines.body: Don't interrupt unnecessarily — offer help subtly, waiting for interaction rather than a demanding pop-up.

contentGuidelines.title: Ensure Accessibility
contentGuidelines.body: All helper text should be screen reader compatible and keyboard navigable. Don't rely on colour alone for meaning.

modal-basic.use: Modals are temporary overlays used for important tasks like confirmations or forms. They must include a clear title, concise content, and actions, with easy ways to close (button, Esc key, or tapping outside). Modals should trap focus for accessibility and use smooth animations. On mobile, they adapt to full-width or slide-up styles.
anatomy: The anatomy includes a header with a clear title and a close button, a body section with a heading and supporting text, and a footer holding the primary and secondary action buttons (Cancel and Confirm). The whole modal sits in a central container over a dimmed background overlay.
1. Dialog Title, 2. Section Heading, 3. Dialog Body/Content, 4. Cancel Button, 5. Close Icon, 6. Dialog Separator, 7. Scrollbar, 8. Modal component, 9. Primary Action Button (Confirm)
size: All modals use a max width of 600px, not 320px, to support readability and layout flexibility

Modal spacing (tokens): title top padding spacing/md; title-to-heading spacing/md; heading top margin spacing/md; heading-to-body spacing/lg; body bottom padding spacing/md; button area top margin spacing/md; button area bottom padding spacing/md; left/right modal padding spacing/md; button horizontal gap spacing/sm; right button padding spacing/md
Modal buttons: padding top/bottom spacing/sm, padding left/right spacing/md

Modal forms: heading top padding spacing/md; heading-to-label spacing/md; option-to-option spacing/md; form-fields-to-paragraph spacing/md; bottom/right modal padding spacing/md; option padding top/bottom spacing/sm, left spacing/sm; checkbox-to-option-text gap spacing/sm

types.title: Modal/warning
types.body: Used to alert users to critical or potentially destructive actions (e.g. deleting an item, exiting without saving). Clear, concise messaging with strong visual hierarchy — often an attention-grabbing icon or colour. Include a descriptive title, an explanation of the consequence, and clear action buttons — typically a primary (e.g. "Delete") and a secondary (e.g. "Cancel"). Must be easily dismissible and accessible.

types.title: Modal/scrollable
types.body: For longer content (policy information, product details, terms and conditions) without overwhelming screen space. Vertical scrolling should be enabled within the modal body, not the background. Title stays fixed at the top; action buttons remain visible or easily accessible.

types.title: Modal/forms
types.body: For short, focused user input tasks. Structured with a clear heading, form labels, fields, and submit/cancel buttons. Use inline validation and helpful error messaging. All form elements properly labelled and accessible with a logical tab order.

behaviour: Modals appear in response to a user action and take focus immediately on opening. While open, interaction is limited to the modal — background content is dimmed and inaccessible via a backdrop and focus trap. Dismissible via a visible close button and Escape, unless a critical task requires completion. Focus returns to the triggering element on close. Modals should not stack, and transitions should be smooth and fast.
If showing critical information, provide an "x" to close. If a critical user response is required, don't include the "x" — the user should make an input action, either "Cancel" or "Confirm".
accessibility: Properly announced by screen readers, with focus trapped inside while open and dismissible via Escape
Use semantic HTML (<dialog> or <div> with role="dialog"), label with aria-labelledby and aria-describedby, and keep a logical focus order
Don't rely solely on visual cues — include clear labels and instructions, and give keyboard-only users full control to open, navigate, and close
doList: Use modals for focused, short interactions (confirmations, alerts, quick forms)
Always provide a clear title and concise content
Trap keyboard focus and support Escape to dismiss
Return focus to the triggering element once closed
Dim the background to help focus
dontList: Overuse modals or rely on them for complex workflows or critical information that could be missed
Launch modals without user action (e.g. on page load)
Stack multiple modals on top of each other
Block users from closing the modal unless absolutely necessary
Use vague or overly complex language inside the modal

contentGuidelines.title: Start with a clear, specific title
contentGuidelines.body: e.g. "Delete Item", not a vague "Alert" or "Attention".

contentGuidelines.title: Write purpose-driven body content
contentGuidelines.body: Explain what's happening, why it matters, and what's expected. e.g. "Are you sure you want to permanently delete this file? This action cannot be undone."

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear, action-oriented button labels
contentGuidelines.body: "Delete", "Save Changes", "Continue Without Saving" — not "OK" or "Yes".

contentGuidelines.title: Support cancellation or dismissal
contentGuidelines.body: Always provide a secondary button ("Cancel"/"Back") and explain the effect of cancelling if progress would be lost.

contentGuidelines.title: Use supporting text for context or warnings
contentGuidelines.body: For irreversible actions, add a brief supporting paragraph; use bold/colour sparingly to highlight warnings.

contentGuidelines.title: Be concise, especially on small screens
contentGuidelines.body: A few sentences at most — avoid decorative language or lengthy terms and conditions.

contentGuidelines.title: Maintain a logical content hierarchy
contentGuidelines.body: Title, then supporting text, then actions — most important information first.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid overloading with too many actions
contentGuidelines.body: Two or three options maximum, usually a primary and a secondary button.

contentGuidelines.title: Match tone to context
contentGuidelines.body: Calm and neutral for standard interactions, direct for urgent alerts, friendly for onboarding tips.

contentGuidelines.title: Use inline links or tooltips for additional info
contentGuidelines.body: Keep the core message clean; put help text or legal references behind an optional link/tooltip.

promo-card.use: Cards display content and actions about a single subject. Cards are containers used to group and present related information and actions about a single subject, helping users quickly scan and compare options or content.
anatomy: Promo Card, Promo Card Heading, Paragraph, Card promo image
accessibility: Cards can be non-actionable containers that include buttons or links, or directly actionable without containing other interactive elements — avoid stacking interactions by placing actions on an already-actionable surface
Tab: on directly actionable cards, moves to the next card; on non-actionable cards with buttons/links, moves to the next actionable element
Space or Enter confirms the focused action

contentGuidelines.title: Accommodate content, don't constrain it
contentGuidelines.body: Let card height grow naturally with the text. Prioritise clarity over fixed-size consistency.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid truncating important content with ellipses
contentGuidelines.body: Truncation makes content harder to understand, inaccessible to screen readers, and inconsistent across cards of varying content lengths.

transitions: Cards use a container transform pattern to reveal additional content when expanded — cards don't flip over to reveal information

card-cover-type.use: Cards display content and actions about a single subject — grouping related information so users can quickly scan and compare options.
anatomy: Approximate mapping — no exact real capture of a generic "Basic Card" exists yet. Basic Card anatomy per the source: Heading, Content Bundle (icon, label, paragraph, link label), optional Button Section, optional Image placeholder.
accessibility: Cards can be non-actionable containers that include buttons or links, or directly actionable without containing other interactive elements — avoid stacking interactions
Tab: directly actionable cards move to the next card; non-actionable cards with buttons/links move to the next actionable element
Space or Enter confirms the focused action

contentGuidelines.title: Accommodate content, don't constrain it
contentGuidelines.body: Let card height grow naturally with the text rather than forcing fixed-size consistency.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid truncating important content with ellipses
contentGuidelines.body: Truncation makes content harder to understand and inaccessible to screen readers.

transitions: Container transform pattern to reveal additional content when expanded — cards don't flip

nav-side-parent.use: Navigation in a design system includes reusable components like headers, sidebars, and menus that help users move through an interface easily. It ensures consistency, supports wayfinding, and defines behaviour across devices. RAA's navigation is clear, responsive, and structured — primary links with icons, optional sub-navigation, and active state highlights, adapting to a collapsible menu on mobile.
anatomy: 1. Parent Menu Icon, 2. Parent Menu Item (Expanded), 3. Parent Menu Item (Collapsed), 4. Parent Menu Item (Default), 5. Menu Group Container, 6. Expand/Collapse Icon, 7. Child Menu Items
Side drawer: 1. Close Button, 2. Log Out Button — the rest is the same as the standard side nav
typography: Menu parent icon — Font Awesome 6 Pro/18px | 24px
Menu open/close icon — Font Awesome 6 Pro/16px | 22px

types.title: Navigation
types.body: Provides clear access to key sections with top-level items and optional submenus. Icons sit 8px from labels, with consistent vertical spacing and 24px side padding. Items are vertically aligned, touch-friendly, and keyboard accessible.

types.title: Navigation side
types.body: Side navigation anchors the layout with a vertical menu. Parent items expand to show indented child links. Spacing is consistent for readability, supporting clear hierarchy, responsiveness, and accessibility.

behaviour: Menus open and close with a subtle, responsive animation — 200–300ms, ease-in-out. Expanding: child items fade and slide down slightly. Collapsing reverses this motion, avoiding abrupt changes.
tokens: Top margin to first item — spacing/lg
Bottom margin below last item — spacing/lg
Side drawer — spacing/md padding top (close icon), spacing/sm padding top (log out button)
accessibility: Fully accessible for assistive technology users — each menu item is keyboard navigable with clear focus states
Expandable sections use aria-expanded and aria-controls to convey state to screen readers
Icons are paired with descriptive labels so meaning is conveyed both visually and audibly
Close and logout buttons are easily reachable with descriptive aria-labels
All interactive elements follow a logical tab order
doList: Use plain language for menu labels
Let icons support, not replace, text
Follow ARIA best practice for expandable items
Keep navigation operable by keyboard alone with visible focus indicators
Maintain a logical, predictable structure
dontList: Rely solely on icons or bury key features deep in hidden submenus
Overload the navigation with too many options
Skip accessibility considerations like colour contrast or screen reader labels
Use inconsistent terminology

contentGuidelines.title: Be consistent across platforms
contentGuidelines.body: Keep placement, behaviour, and styling consistent across devices to reduce cognitive effort.

contentGuidelines.title: Prioritise clarity over cleverness
contentGuidelines.body: Use simple, recognisable labels — avoid jargon or playful ambiguity.

contentGuidelines.title: Limit primary navigation items
contentGuidelines.body: Keep top-level navigation to 5–7 core items; use secondary/mega menus for deeper structures.

contentGuidelines.title: Use visual hierarchy to show relationships
contentGuidelines.body: Indentation, font weight, size, or spacing to differentiate parent items from sub-items.

contentGuidelines.title: Ensure responsive behaviour
contentGuidelines.body: Hamburger menus, bottom nav bars, or collapsible drawers on small screens; full navigation on larger ones.

contentGuidelines.title: Highlight the current location
contentGuidelines.body: Bold text, underlines, selected states, or breadcrumb trails so users know where they are.

contentGuidelines.title: Use descriptive icons with labels
contentGuidelines.body: Icons speed recognition but should be paired with text unless universally understood (e.g. a house icon for "Home").

pagination.use: Pagination breaks content into pages for easier navigation. Include clear page numbers, next/previous buttons, and highlight the current page. Ensure it's accessible with keyboard support and aria-labels. Use when users need to browse or return to specific content easily.
anatomy: Pagination includes previous/next buttons, page numbers with the current page highlighted, and optional ellipses or first/last buttons. Elements are evenly spaced in a container.
1. Previous Button, 2. First Page Number, 3. Ellipsis, 4. Next Button, 5. Pagination Bar
size: Internal padding: 11px top, 13px left, 11px bottom, 13px right

types.title: Pagination
types.body: Divides content into multiple pages, typically with page numbers or Previous/Next buttons, helping users navigate large datasets or articles in manageable sections.

types.title: Pagination (Previous and next icons only)
types.body: Shows only two icons for moving between pages — good for mobile or minimalist designs, and linear content like articles or image galleries where exact page numbers aren't necessary.

behaviour: Dynamic updates — content updates immediately on page selection
Disabled states — Previous/Next disabled when not applicable (first/last page)
Visible feedback — current page highlighted with background colour P2/30
Smooth, fast transitions
Keyboard and touch-friendly controls
accessibility: Keyboard navigation (Tab, Enter, arrow keys) and screen reader support
Semantic HTML — <nav> with aria-label="Pagination", <ul> for structure
Current page indicated with aria-current="page"
Clear aria-labels on buttons/links (e.g. "Go to page 3")
Visible focus states; large enough touch targets
doList: Show the current page clearly, with aria-current="page"
Include Previous/Next buttons, disabled when not needed
Use ellipses to collapse long page ranges
Keep every visible page number clickable
Support full keyboard navigation
Use descriptive ARIA labels
Design for responsiveness
dontList: Clutter the interface with too many visible pages
Rely solely on colour to indicate the current page
Hide important controls on smaller screens
Use infinite scrolling when users need to return to a specific page
Neglect accessibility labelling

contentGuidelines.title: Show the current page clearly
contentGuidelines.body: Different colour, bold text, or background highlight, plus aria-current="page" for screen readers.

contentGuidelines.title: Include Previous and Next buttons
contentGuidelines.body: Disable them when not needed (first/last page) to avoid confusion.

contentGuidelines.title: Use ellipses for long lists
contentGuidelines.body: Collapse the middle pages to reduce visual clutter while showing more exist.

contentGuidelines.title: Keep page numbers clickable
contentGuidelines.body: Let users jump directly to a page rather than clicking through sequentially.

contentGuidelines.title: Support keyboard navigation
contentGuidelines.body: Tab, Enter, and arrow keys should all work.

contentGuidelines.title: Use descriptive ARIA labels
contentGuidelines.body: e.g. aria-label="Go to page 4".

contentGuidelines.title: Design for responsiveness
contentGuidelines.body: Simplify controls on smaller devices without losing usability.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid overloading with too many pages
contentGuidelines.body: Limit visible page links to keep the experience user-friendly.

popup-menu.use: A popup menu is a temporary, contextual menu that appears near a triggering element to show related actions. It should be concise, easy to navigate with keyboard, and dismissible by clicking outside or pressing Esc. Use smooth transitions for a polished experience.
anatomy: A popup menu includes a trigger (icon or button), a container, and a list of menu items. Items may have text, icons, or shortcuts, positioned near the trigger with clear boundaries and states for hover, focus, and active.
1. Title/Header, 2. Popup container bubble point, 3. Close Icon, 4. Title, 5. Description, 6. Icon, 7. Popup/Modal Container

types.title: Support contact modal
types.body: A centred overlay providing immediate access to help options (e.g. live chat, phone support), typically triggered by a "Help"/"Contact Us" button, temporarily blocking background interaction.

behaviour: Opens as a modal with a fade-and-slide-up animation, 200–300ms, ease-out. Closes with a fade-and-slide-down animation, 150–250ms, ease-in. All transitions must be interruptible and accessible.
tokens: Gap icon-to-text within a sub-header — spacing/lg
accessibility: Triggered as a modal dialog that traps keyboard focus until dismissed, preventing background interaction
The heading is a semantic heading (e.g. <h2>) for screen reader context
Interactive options are focusable buttons/links with clear, descriptive labels
The close button is keyboard-accessible with an aria-label (e.g. "Close popup")
Icons are decorative or carry aria-hidden="true" where appropriate; essential info (like hours) is plain text
doList: Include a clear, descriptive heading that communicates the popup's purpose
Make interactive elements easily navigable by keyboard and screen reader, with proper ARIA roles/labels
Trap focus within the popup while it's open
Provide a visible, clearly labelled close button
Ensure high contrast, readable text, and support for text resizing
dontList: Rely on icons alone — pair with supporting text or accessible labels
Prevent users from closing the popup or navigating without a mouse
Overload the popup with too much information
Allow interaction with background content while the popup is active
Assume all users share the same input methods or abilities

contentGuidelines.title: Be clear and concise
contentGuidelines.body: Plain language, short sentences, key information first.

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear headings
contentGuidelines.body: A friendly, helpful heading that sets context, e.g. "Got a question? We can help".

contentGuidelines.title: Guide the user
contentGuidelines.body: Clear actions with short, direct labels and supporting text explaining what happens next.

contentGuidelines.title: Respect tone and brand voice
contentGuidelines.body: Friendly, professional, reassuring — especially during problem-solving.

contentGuidelines.title: Prioritise important information
contentGuidelines.body: Contact details, hours, or help options in a logical order; bold key parts like phone numbers.

contentGuidelines.title: Support accessibility
contentGuidelines.body: Avoid overly complex language; add aria-labels where needed; don't embed text in images.

contentGuidelines.title: Keep it focused
contentGuidelines.body: One clear purpose per popup — don't overload with marketing or unrelated content.

radio-basic.use: Radio buttons let users select one option from a group. Only one can be chosen at a time, and selecting a new option deselects the previous one. Each button should have a clear label and be grouped with a descriptive heading.
variants: Desktop, simple Yes/No: radios can be horizontally stacked; combined width 282px with 24px horizontal padding between them
Desktop, Yes/No/longer options: radios can be vertically stacked, full width
Mobile: vertically stacked and full width
anatomy: A radio button consists of a circular input icon (filled when selected, empty when not), a label describing the option, and is grouped with other radio buttons under a group label or fieldset title. Supports keyboard navigation, focus states, and mutually-exclusive selection.
1. Radio Button Icon, 2. Field Label
size: Horizontal layouts — at least 16px between options
Spacing between buttons and helper/error text — 8px
states: Default — unselected, hollow circular icon with a readable label, fully interactive
Focus — a visible focus indicator (e.g. a ring/outline) appears when navigated to via keyboard
Selected — a filled inner circle appears; selecting one automatically deselects any other option in the group
Disabled — greyed out or reduced opacity, cannot be clicked, focused, or keyboard-navigated
Error — the whole group (not just one button) shows a red border/icon/underline plus a clear error message nearby
accessibility: Keyboard accessible with arrow-key navigation between options
Group using a semantic <fieldset> with a <legend> for context
Use appropriate ARIA roles for custom components; visible focus indicators
Screen readers should announce the group name, selected option, and total number of choices
doList: Group related radio buttons under a clear label or question
Give each option a descriptive, concise label
Keep the number of options manageable — ideally no more than 5–7
Support arrow-key navigation with visible focus indicators
dontList: Use radio buttons when multiple selections are needed — use checkboxes instead
Use them for binary Yes/No choices — a toggle switch fits better
Leave options unlabeled or ungrouped
Overlook accessibility — the group context and selected option must be announced

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear, descriptive labels
contentGuidelines.body: Describe the actual value or action, not vague terms like "Option 1".

contentGuidelines.title: Use sentence case
contentGuidelines.body: "Email notifications", not title case.

contentGuidelines.title: Group with a meaningful question or prompt
contentGuidelines.body: e.g. "How would you like to be contacted?" — improves context and screen reader accessibility.

contentGuidelines.title: Limit the number of options
contentGuidelines.body: No more than 5–7; use a dropdown for longer lists.

contentGuidelines.title: Make options mutually exclusive
contentGuidelines.body: If multiple selections are possible, use checkboxes instead.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid default selection unless necessary
contentGuidelines.body: Preselecting only when there's a clear benefit or it matches a user's prior input.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid "Other" without clarification
contentGuidelines.body: Pair it with a text field so users can add detail.

contentGuidelines.title: Support accessibility with fieldsets and legends
contentGuidelines.body: Wrap groups in semantic <fieldset>/<legend>.

contentGuidelines.title: Be consistent in wording and structure
contentGuidelines.body: Keep phrasing parallel across labels.

contentGuidelines.title: Use tooltips or help text sparingly
contentGuidelines.body: Only when the label truly can't stand alone.
