tokens: Gap between radio icon and field label — spacing/sm
Radio horizontal — top/bottom/left/right padding all spacing/sm

radio-tile.use: Radio Tiles are a stylised version of radio buttons that let users choose one option from a set. Each option appears as a clickable card or tile, often with text, icons, or images, and highlights visually when selected. They're ideal for mobile and visually rich interfaces.
anatomy: Radio Tiles present one selectable option per tile in a visual, tile-based layout, supporting titles, descriptions, or icons. Only one tile can be selected at a time, with clear states for hover, focus, and selection.
1. Radio Button, 2. Thumbnail/Image Placeholder, 3. Title
states: Default — unselected, radio button, optional image/icon, and title, with a neutral border
Clicked/Selected — the radio button fills and the tile border turns green as confirmation
Disabled — non-interactive, dimmed/faded, cannot be selected
Focus — a clear focus indicator (outline or border glow) on keyboard/assistive-tech focus
Error — border or radio highlighted in an error colour (usually red), with an optional nearby error message
accessibility: Use role="radio" within a radiogroup, with aria-checked to indicate selection
Include a clear group label via aria-label or aria-labelledby
Fully keyboard-navigable with arrow keys, with a visible focus indicator
Minimum tap target 44×44px; the whole tile should be clickable, not just the radio input
WCAG colour contrast; selection must never rely on colour alone
doList: Make the entire tile clickable, not just the radio button
Use clear, concise, meaningful labels
Support keyboard arrow-key navigation with a visible focus state
Indicate the selected state both visually and programmatically
dontList: Rely on colour alone to indicate selection or status
Use touch targets smaller than 44×44px
Remove or hide focus outlines
Allow multiple selection — tiles are single-choice
Let long/wrapped labels break the layout
Omit ARIA attributes assistive tech relies on

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear and descriptive titles
contentGuidelines.body: The title is the primary decision-making cue — avoid vague terms like "Standard" or "Option 1".

contentGuidelines.title: Keep content concise and scannable
contentGuidelines.body: Short sentences or phrases, most important info first.

contentGuidelines.title: Support with optional subtext only when needed
contentGuidelines.body: Clarify distinctions like price tiers or durations, only if essential.

contentGuidelines.title: Use visuals to reinforce, not replace, text
contentGuidelines.body: Icons/thumbnails help recognition but must be paired with meaningful text.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid jargon and technical language
contentGuidelines.body: Rephrase internal/business terms into plain, user-friendly language.

contentGuidelines.title: Ensure consistency across tiles
contentGuidelines.body: Same structure — title, optional subtext, visual position — across a group.

contentGuidelines.title: Use parallel sentence structure
contentGuidelines.body: If one tile starts with a verb, the others should too.

contentGuidelines.title: Keep tone neutral and informative
contentGuidelines.body: Radio Tiles are decision tools, not promotional banners.

contentGuidelines.title: Limit content per tile to one clear message
contentGuidelines.body: One core idea or value proposition per tile.

contentGuidelines.title: Test on multiple screen sizes
contentGuidelines.body: Avoid awkward wrapping or truncation; set max character limits where needed.

tokens: Gap between image and title — spacing-md

section-title.use: A section title clearly indicates the beginning of a new content group within a page or interface. It helps users quickly understand the topic or purpose of the section, improving content scanability and accessibility. Typically styled with larger or bold typography, section titles establish visual hierarchy and support content structure across different screen sizes.
anatomy: The text label (defining the section's purpose), typography (larger size, bold weight), spacing (padding/margin for separation), alignment (usually left-aligned), and sometimes a supporting icon or divider.
1. Title/Header

types.title: Primary section title
types.body: Currently the only type — bold, large, and highly visible to help users quickly identify main content areas. Provides clear structure and hierarchy for scanning and accessibility. Should be styled consistently across pages, using language that reflects the content that follows so both users and screen readers understand the page's layout.

accessibility: Use a semantic <h2> heading to convey structure to assistive technologies
Follow a logical heading order — never skip levels
Sufficient colour contrast; hierarchy must be programmatically determinable, not just visual
doList: Use semantic heading tags for proper structure
Keep titles short, descriptive, and meaningful
Maintain visual consistency in typography, size, and spacing
Ensure sufficient colour contrast
dontList: Use visual style alone (size/colour) to indicate importance without semantic markup
Skip heading levels (e.g. <h2> straight to <h4>)
Use vague or generic labels like "Section 1"
Use all-caps unless stylistically necessary and still readable
Place interactive elements inside section titles unless clearly labelled and accessible

contentGuidelines.title: Text and contents
contentGuidelines.body: Concise and descriptive (ideally 1–5 words); consistent title/sentence case; avoid vague terms like "Content Area".

contentGuidelines.title: Structure and semantics
contentGuidelines.body: Semantic heading tags, no skipped levels; only one <h1> per page, with section titles starting at <h2>.

contentGuidelines.title: Visual style
contentGuidelines.body: Larger, bolder than body text; adequate spacing above/below; left-aligned unless the layout requires otherwise; dividers/icons only if they support clarity.

select.use: The select option lets users choose one item from a dropdown list. It includes a label, a dropdown icon, and a list of clear, concise options. It supports keyboard navigation, focus states, and screen readers for full accessibility.
anatomy: A label describing the field, a selected value area showing the chosen option or placeholder, and a dropdown icon indicating expandability. When opened, a dropdown menu shows selectable options. Optional helper text or error messages appear below.
1. Field label, 2. Select option, 3. Pull-down icon
Option states: 1. Option not selected, 2. Option selected, 3. Option component
accessibility: Clear, associated label for screen readers
Semantic <select>/<option>, or ARIA combobox/listbox/option roles for custom components
Keyboard navigation for opening the menu, moving between options, and selecting
Visible focus indicators; all states (hover, focus, selected, error) meet WCAG AA contrast
Error messages and helper text connected via aria-describedby
doList: Provide clear, descriptive labels
Keep option text brief and scannable
Organise choices logically — alphabetically or by relevance
Use clear placeholders to prompt selection
Display error messages near the field
Maintain sufficient contrast across all states
Use tooltips for unfamiliar terms where needed
dontList: Use select fields to trigger actions — reserve them for choosing values
Overwhelm users with too many choices without grouping
Rely solely on colour to indicate status
Leave confusing default selections that risk unintended submissions
Hide key options inside unlabelled opt-groups
tokens: Gap option to input component — spacing/xs

contentGuidelines.title: Use clear, descriptive labels
contentGuidelines.body: Users should immediately understand what they're selecting.

contentGuidelines.title: Keep option text short and scannable
contentGuidelines.body: Especially important on mobile.

contentGuidelines.title: Order options logically
contentGuidelines.body: Alphabetically, numerically, or by relevance.

contentGuidelines.title: Use placeholder text thoughtfully
contentGuidelines.body: e.g. "Select an option" — never as a permanent value.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid ambiguous options
contentGuidelines.body: Avoid vague terms like "Other" unless followed by clarification.

contentGuidelines.title: Group related options clearly
contentGuidelines.body: Use headings or separators for long lists.

contentGuidelines.title: Provide additional context when needed
contentGuidelines.body: Tooltips or help text for options needing explanation.

contentGuidelines.title: Match terms to user language
contentGuidelines.body: Avoid internal jargon.

contentGuidelines.title: Be consistent across the product
contentGuidelines.body: Same terminology and ordering everywhere select fields appear.

contentGuidelines.title: Support accessibility in wording
contentGuidelines.body: Option text should make sense read aloud by a screen reader.

table.use: Tables display structured data in rows and columns for easy comparison and scanning. In a design system, they should be clear, accessible, and responsive, with consistent spacing, readable text, and support for sorting, filtering, and pagination when needed.
anatomy: Clear headers, aligned columns, and consistent cell spacing. Header rows carry labels, with optional sorting or tooltips. Rows support scanning, selection, or actions.
1. Label, 2. Title, 3. Paragraph, 4. External link with icon, 5. Paragraph details, 6. Table Container

types.title: Bordered table
types.body: spacing/md (24px) padding, 1px solid border using the P2/100 colour token, 4px radius. Best for compact layouts, cards, or modular components where the table should be visually distinct from surrounding content.

types.title: Divider table (borderless)
types.body: spacing/md (24px) padding, no outer border/radius, a 1px P2/50 divider between stacked tables/sections. Best for clean, open layouts like dashboards or lists.

accessibility: Semantic table elements — <table>, <thead>, <tbody>, <th>, <td>
Descriptive headers using <th scope> to link data cells to their headers
Keyboard navigation through rows and interactive elements (sorting, pagination)
Sufficient colour contrast; never rely on colour alone
Captions or summaries for scrollable/complex tables
doList: Use clear, concise headers with consistent alignment
Use enough padding to avoid clutter; alternate row colours starting S2/30 then P3/100
Use semantic HTML and support full keyboard navigation
Include sorting/filtering/pagination for large datasets
Make tables responsive — horizontal scroll or stacked layout on small screens
dontList: Cram too much data into a single table
Rely on colour alone to convey meaning
Use non-semantic elements (e.g. <div>) for table structure
Hide critical information on smaller screens
Omit a clear empty state when there's no data

contentGuidelines.title: Be clear and concise
contentGuidelines.body: Short, descriptive column headers — not vague terms like "Info" or "Data".

contentGuidelines.title: Keep labels simple
contentGuidelines.body: Plain language; only universally-understood abbreviations.

contentGuidelines.title: Align text properly
contentGuidelines.body: Left-align text, right-align numbers for easy comparison.

contentGuidelines.title: Use consistent formatting
contentGuidelines.body: Same date format, currency symbols and decimals throughout.

contentGuidelines.title: Limit text length
contentGuidelines.body: Truncate with ellipses; use tooltips or expandable rows for more detail.

contentGuidelines.title: Avoid overloading
contentGuidelines.body: Prioritise essential content; use progressive disclosure for secondary info.

contentGuidelines.title: Support empty states
contentGuidelines.body: e.g. "No items found. Try adjusting your filters."

behaviour: Hover/focus states for clickable rows; prefer buttons/links within cells over full-row clicks
Sorting with visible icons; dynamic filtering with clear feedback
Expandable rows for inline detail; pagination or lazy loading with loading indicators and result counts
Helpful messages for empty/error states
External links clearly labelled (e.g. with a ↗ icon), open in a new tab with target="_blank" and rel="noopener noreferrer"

textarea.use: Use text area so users can enter multiple lines of text. Text area is used when information longer than a single line of text is needed or expected — for example, comments fields.
variants: Default, invalid
anatomy: Label
Container
Text (optional)
Description (optional)
Character count (optional)
size: 6px spacing between label, container and description
typography: Default — Label Medium/14px|20px P2/100; Text Regular/14px|20px P2/100; Description Regular/12px|18px P2/50; Character count Regular/12px|18px P2/50
Invalid: Invalid/100. Valid: Valid/100. Disabled: P2/40.
characterLimit: Only use a character count when there's a good reason — legal, technical, or evidence users will give more text than needed
transitions: Animation on active and focus states
arrangement: 24px margin between the text area and nearby components
Text area container should fill the width of its parent
accessibility: Avoid placeholder text where possible — it disappears once typing starts, isn't always read by screen readers, and often lacks contrast
doList: Always use a label
Specify character counts when required
Announce inline validation errors and focus the field in error
Keep tab order logical
Give specific error messages that explain the fix
dontList: Use a text area without a label
Truncate text — make it scrollable instead
Use an asterisk for mandatory/optional — write '(optional)' in the label
Use a text area for succinct responses like email addresses or names — use an input field instead
Disable copy and paste
Set a max container height (support dynamic text sizing)
Hijack the cursor during input
Set a min/max input limit without stating it in the character count
Use hint text that isn't relevant or meaningful
Use placeholder text to give instructions
Write ambiguous error messages that don't explain the fix

toggle.use: Toggles are used to switch between two mutually exclusive states, "on" and "off", and are best suited to system and settings functionality (e.g. enabling windscreen coverage for an insurance policy, or turning on account notifications).
variants: Toggle (Desktop) — default size, optimised for cursor interactions
Toggle LG (Mobile) — larger touch target for improved accessibility on touch devices
anatomy: Track — the background path, indicating on/off state via colour
Thumb — the handle the user interacts with
Icon — a check or cross icon indicating the on/off state
typography: Font Awesome Pro for the state icons — Toggle Regular/12px, P3/100 (default/focus), P2/30 (disabled); Toggle LG Regular/14px, same colours
states: Focus — visible focus ring/highlight on keyboard navigation
transitions: Track colour fades to match the new state
accessibility: Use role="switch" for semantic clarity
Include aria-checked="true/false"
Labels clearly associated via <label for="id">
Sufficient colour contrast for both states
Focus states visible and meeting contrast requirements
doList: Use for a binary choice, e.g. enabling/disabling notifications
Use when changes take effect immediately, without further confirmation
Pair toggles with clear labels
Use consistent placement across the UI
Test for keyboard accessibility and screen reader compatibility
dontList: Use for actions that require confirmation or submission
Use for choices between more than two options — use radio buttons instead
Overload the interface with toggles for unrelated options
Use without sufficient colour contrast or indicators between states
tokens: Icon font — font/family/icon; icon size — size/toggle/icon/small or size/toggle/icon/large
